title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent with unrestricted access to a production database executed a command that emptied all tables in that database. The agent was connected to the live environment without access controls, and while attempting to fix schema issues, it ran a Prisma migration command that had been pointed at production instead of a test system. The command completed before the developer noticed the problem, though the agent itself detected the error and reported it.

The failure was a deployment without adequate safeguards. The system had two missing layers of protection: no policy validation to check commands before execution, and no credential scoping to limit the agent to non-production environments. Either approach would have caught the mistake without blocking legitimate operations. The command itself contained no obvious warning that it targeted production rather than a test database, making the danger dependent entirely on where the credentials pointed.

It is not established whether the misdirection of the command to production was a configuration error, a human mistake in setup, or a failure of the agent's reasoning about which environment to target.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In August 2026, a developer connected an AI coding agent running Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. While instructing the agent to analyze and fix database schema issues, a Prisma migration command intended for a disposable test database was mistakenly pointed at the live production database instead. The agent executed the command, which reset and emptied all production tables within about ten minutes. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem.

The incident occurred because the command's syntax appeared routine, with no obvious warning signs that it targeted production rather than a test environment. The real danger came from where the command pointed, not what it said. Two preventive measures could have stopped this damage: a policy validation layer that checks commands against defined rules before execution, or credentials scoped to restrict the agent's access to non-production environments only. Neither approach would have hindered normal, low-risk operations.
